messages.author: dc06e9781ae0ecac
messages.subject: Restricted parameter space
parts:
Hello,

I'm trying to mimic the following BUGS code in STAN:

model {
for (i in 1:N){
pp[i] <- exp(b0 + b1 * X1[i] + b2*X2[i])
Y[i] ~ dbern(pp[i])
}
b0 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
b1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
b2 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
# implementing the constrains for each observation in the data
for (i in 1:N){
ones[i] <- 1
ones[i] ~ dbern(C1[i])
C1[i] <- step(1-pp[i])
}
}

It is from Chu and Cole's paper "Estimation of Risk Ratios in Cohort Studies With Common Outcomes".

To do the constraints for each observation in the data, I based my code on the STAN versions of the Funshapes examples. So I ran the following code (the data is from the example 1 of the same paper):

library(rstan)

x = seq(1,10)
y = c(rep(0,4),1,0,rep(1,4))

dados = list(N = 10, Y = y, X1 = x)

inits <- function(){
    list(alpha0 = 0, alpha1 = 0)
    list(alpha0 = -1, alpha1 = -1)
    list(alpha0 = -2, alpha1 = 0)
}

logbincode <- '
data {
  int N;
  int Y[N];
  real X1[N];
}

parameters {
  real alpha0;
  real alpha1;
}

transformed parameters {
 real<lower=0,upper=1> p[N] ;

 for (i in 1:N)  {
  p[i] <- exp(alpha0 + alpha1*X1[i]);
 }
}

model {
    alpha0 ~normal(0,100);
    alpha1 ~normal(0,100);

 for (i in 1:N) {
     Y[i] ~ bernoulli(p[i]) ;
  lp__ <- lp__ + log(step(1-p[i]));
     }
}

generated quantities {
 real RR1;

 RR1 <-exp(alpha1) ;
}
'

fit <- stan(model_code = logbincode, data = dados, iter = 1000, chains = 3, init=inits)

When I ran the code, I got lots of the following message:
"Informational Message: The parameter state is about to be Metropolis rejected due to the following underlying, non-fatal (really) issue (and please ignore that what comes next might say 'error'): Invalid value of p: Error in function validate transformed params N4stan5agrad3varE: p[k0__] is 1.0352225089032803:0, but must be less than or equal to 1
If the problem persists across multiple draws, you might have a problem with an initial state or a gradient somewhere.
 If the problem does not persist, the resulting samples will still be drawn from the posterior."

Although the sampling is completed and the results make sense.
If I don't put the "  lp__ <- lp__ + log(step(1-p[i])); ", I got the same messages and resultas that also makes sense.

So I think the constraint is not working and would appreciate any help on this.

Thanks and congratulations for the software.
Vanessa

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Restricted parameter space
parts:
On 10/14/13 3:42 PM, Vanessa Leotti Torman wrote:
> Hello,
>
> I'm trying to mimic the following BUGS code in STAN:
>
> model {
> for (i in 1:N){
> pp[i] <- exp(b0 + b1 * X1[i] + b2*X2[i])
> Y[i] ~ dbern(pp[i])
> }
> b0 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
> b1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
> b2 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
> # implementing the constrains for each observation in the data
> for (i in 1:N){
> ones[i] <- 1
> ones[i] ~ dbern(C1[i])
> C1[i] <- step(1-pp[i])
> }
> }

Could you parse this out for those of us who aren't
BUGS experts? The Bernoulli loop thing is a BUGS hack
for adding arbitrary log probabilty functions. You did correctly translate
this loop into Stan, which just lets you increment directly:
for (i in 1:N)

lp__ <- lp__ + log(step(1-pp[i]));

It's not an efficient approach in BUGS and you've recreated
the same kind of behavior in Stan.

The reason the log(step()) doesn't seem to help with errors is
that we catch it before this stage when you try to send in
a greater than 0 value as a Bernoulli parameter.

> It is from Chu and Cole's paper "Estimation of Risk Ratios in Cohort Studies With Common Outcomes".
>
> To do the constraints for each observation in the data, I based my code on the STAN versions of the Funshapes examples.
> So I ran the following code (the data is from the example 1 of the same paper):
>
> library(rstan)
>
> x = seq(1,10)
> y = c(rep(0,4),1,0,rep(1,4))
>
> dados = list(N = 10, Y = y, X1 = x)
>
> inits <- function(){
> list(alpha0 = 0, alpha1 = 0)
> list(alpha0 = -1, alpha1 = -1)
> list(alpha0 = -2, alpha1 = 0)
> }
>
> logbincode <- '
> data {
> int N;
> int Y[N];
> real X1[N];
> }
>
> parameters {
> real alpha0;
> real alpha1;
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
> real<lower=0,upper=1> p[N] ;
>
> for (i in 1:N) {
> p[i] <- exp(alpha0 + alpha1*X1[i]);

Where did the X2 go? And why rename the b values to alpha?

> }
> }

In Stan, you can declare p and X1 as vectors and
just use:

p <- exp(alpha0 + alpha1 * X1);

But I'm curious as to why you'd do it this way rather
than as a logistic regression. It would probably fix
your issues.

You can do the same thing with the more complicated expression,
too. It's easiest to constrain the intercept.

>
> model {
> alpha0 ~normal(0,100);
> alpha1 ~normal(0,100);

I think this should be normal(0,10), because BUGS uses
precision (1 / sigma^2) and we use scale (sigma).

>
> for (i in 1:N) {
> Y[i] ~ bernoulli(p[i]) ;
> lp__ <- lp__ + log(step(1-p[i]));
> }
> }

The constraint you really seem to want is this:

alpha0 + alpha1*X1[i] < 0 for all i

or equivalently

alpha0 < - alpha1 * X1[i] for all i

If X1 is positive as in your example, you can do this with:

real<upper= min(-alpha1 * X1)> alpha0;

Then nothing gets violated and you can just get rid of the
increment log business, which will just be a constant 0 if
the step function evaluates to 1, which it should now always do
because of the constraint enforcement.

>
> generated quantities {
> real RR1;
>
> RR1 <-exp(alpha1) ;
> }
> '
>
> fit <- stan(model_code = logbincode, data = dados, iter = 1000, chains = 3, init=inits)
>
> When I ran the code, I got lots of the following message:
> "Informational Message: The parameter state is about to be Metropolis rejected due to the following underlying,
> non-fatal (really) issue (and please ignore that what comes next might say 'error'): Invalid value of p: Error in
> function validate transformed params N4stan5agrad3varE: p[k0__] is 1.0352225089032803:0, but must be less than or equal to 1

Why use exp() here rather than inv_logit? exp can go above 1
and is the cause of the problem.

> If the problem persists across multiple draws, you might have a problem with an initial state or a gradient somewhere.
> If the problem does not persist, the resulting samples will still be drawn from the posterior."

This is a Metropolis rejection that happens because you pass
an illegal parameter (one greater than 1) into the bernoulli.

> Although the sampling is completed and the results make sense.
> If I don't put the " lp__ <- lp__ + log(step(1-p[i])); ", I got the same messages and resultas that also makes sense.

This would enforce the same constraint, because if p[i] > 1, then the step function
is 0 and you're adding -infinity to the log probability, which causes
a rejection.

- Bob

use those almost-flat priors because BUGS won't let you

We usually recommend weakly informative priors that don't
assign probability mass outside of where you roughly expect
the parameters to be.

of doing it another way first, but then just did the algebra. You
just have to make sure X1 and -alpha1 are declared before alpha0.

And yes, you can do it with another variable. But if the constraints
get too complicated or vary by element (like censoring points that
vary by element), you'll go outside of Stan's constraint language and then

interesting constraint.
